Using your 10' pressure-treated 2”x4”s, cut them to the exact length between each post. This will be the length of your fence. 

Step 7: Place Intermediate 2”x4” Members on 8' Centers from One End Post, So That They Are Able to Accept the 4'x8' Plywood Panels.

Place intermediate 2”x4” members on 8' centers from one end post. This will allow you to accept 4'x8' plywood panels. 

Step 8: Paint the Outside and Top of the Fence with a Good Outdoor Primer and Paint.

Paint the outside and top of the fence with a good outdoor primer and paint to protect it from the elements. 

Step 9: Cut 8 24” Pieces from One of the Fence Top Rails.

Cut eight 24” pieces from one of the fence top rails. 

Step 10: Drill the Holes with a Drill Press or a Portable Hand Drill.

Drill the holes with a drill press or a portable hand drill. 

Step 11: From the Center of the First Post, Mark Along the Wall Every 10', and Then Mark a Line Using a Framing Square 22” Down the Wall.

From the center of the first post, mark along the wall every 10', and then mark a line using a framing square 22” down the wall. 

Step 12: Secure the Pipe to the Wall Using a 4” Lag Screw and a Thick Washer Between the Pipe and Wall – Do This in Only the Top Hole – Do Not Completely Tighten.

Secure the pipe to the wall using a 4” lag screw and a thick washer between the pipe and wall. Do this in only the top hole and do not completely tighten it at this point. 

Step 13: Once All the Connectors and 118” Top Rail Pipes Have Been Connected, Go Back and Secure the Bottom Lag Screw and Washer and Tighten Both.

Once all the connectors and 118” top rail pipes have been connected, go back and secure the bottom lag screw and washer and tighten both. 

Step 14: Gather Four 56” Top Rail Pipes and Two End Midway Connectors and a Peak Connector.

Gather four 56” top rail pipes and two end midway connectors and a peak connector. 

Step 15: Add a 56” Top Rail Pipe into the Second Wall Connector (1,2).

Add a 56” top rail pipe into the second wall connector (1,2). 

Step 16: Unfold the Cover in a Large Location So That It Can Accommodate the 20'x 30' Size.

Unfold the cover in a large location so that it can accommodate the 20'x 30' size. 

Step 17: Attach 30' Ropes in Three or Four Places Along the Length of the Cover Through the Grommets.

Attach 30' ropes in three or four places along the length of the cover through the grommets. 

Step 18: Pull Each Rope Three or Four Feet, Pulling the Cover over the Framework.

Using a stepladder, secure the center of the cover at the framework's peak using a bungee ball at two locations.

If you're interested in pursuing a career as a strength and conditioning coach, it's important to take the necessary steps to gain the appropriate knowledge and certifications for the job. From taking classes to specializing in certain age groups and sports, here's how to become a successful strength and conditioning coach.

1. Take classes that will prepare you for the job.

The first step to becoming a strength and conditioning coach is to immerse yourself in the field. Attend seminars, workshops, or classes to learn about the latest industry trends and techniques in strength and conditioning training. Look for classes that offer hands-on experience and the opportunity to work with athletes.

2. Decide whether or not you need a certification.

While certification is not always necessary, it can be beneficial in establishing your credibility as a strength and conditioning coach. Research the different certifications available and decide which one(s) are right for you.

3. Choose an organization to get certified through.

Once you've decided on certification, research the different organizations and choose the one that is most reputable and widely recognized within the industry.

4. Find out how much money you'll have to pay to take the certification exam.

Certification exams can be expensive, so make sure you budget accordingly and plan ahead.

5. Prepare for and take the certification exam.

Study extensively and familiarize yourself with the exam format. Practice taking sample exams and work with a coach or mentor to help you prepare.

6. Specialize your activities for the age group you’re working with.

Different age groups require different types of training, so it's important to specialize your activities for the group you'll be working with.

7. Have your athletes stretch out thoroughly before and after exercising to reduce the chances of injury.

Stretching is key to preventing injuries and should be a standard part of every athlete's training routine.

8. Create a program of exercises that will be best suited to the sport your athletes play.

Different sports require different types of conditioning, so tailor your program to the specific needs of each athlete.

9. Create a list of exercises to develop your athletes' core strength.

Core strength is essential in all sports and can help athletes prevent injuries and perform better.

10. Put your athletes through exercises that develop arm strength.

Depending on the sport, arm strength can be crucial for success. Develop exercises that target the arms and improve performance.

11. Develop your athletes' leg strength.

Strong legs are essential in most sports and can help athletes run faster, jump higher, and have more endurance.

12. For injured athletes who need rehabilitation, create a list of isometric exercises, also known as holding moves or holding positions.

Isometric exercises can help injured athletes alleviate pain and regain strength. Make sure you have a wide variety of exercises available to suit each athlete's individual needs.

13. Strengthen your rhetorical awareness.

To be an effective coach, it's important to be able to communicate effectively with your athletes. Work on your communication skills and learn how to effectively convey your message.

14. Negotiate the relationship between your role as author, the message you're trying to send, and the audience that's listening to you.

Understand the different perspectives of your athletes and learn how to tailor your message appropriately.

15. Make use of the rhetorical triangle to make effective arguments.

The rhetorical triangle consists of ethos, pathos, and logos. Learn how to use each effectively to make persuasive arguments and communicate with your athletes.

By following these steps, you can become a successful strength and conditioning coach and help your athletes achieve their full potential.

Playing handbells can be a great way to make music and connect with others who share a passion for these unique instruments. If you're interested in joining a handbell choir or simply learning how to play handbells, you're in luck - with a few basic skills and some practice, you can master these beautiful instruments.

1. Find a handbell choir in your area. Handbell choirs can be found in many communities, and joining one can be a great way to learn from experienced players and make new friends who share your interest in music.

2. Know some basic music fundamentals, or be prepared to learn them fairly quickly. While playing handbells requires some specific techniques, it's important to have a solid foundation in music theory and notation. If you're new to music, consider taking a class or working with a private instructor to learn the basics.

3. Understand the basic idea of a handbell choir. In a handbell choir, each player is responsible for playing a specific set of notes, creating a unique sound that is greater than the sum of its parts. Understanding the role you play in the group dynamic is essential to playing well and working effectively with your fellow musicians.

4. Familiarize yourself with the anatomy of a handbell. Handbells consist of several parts, including the handle, the clapper (which strikes the inside of the bell to produce sound), and the bell rim.

5. Begin by putting on gloves (worn by most choirs to avoid smudging or tarnishing the handbells) and picking up two bells and holding them in front of your chest, either angling towards you or facing straight up, depending on the way your choir has chosen to stand with the bells up.

6. To ring one bell, move it forward by extending it away from your body in a circular motion, with the handle moving slightly ahead of the bell. Damp the bell by touching it lightly to your chest when you complete the circle. Repeat until you are comfortable with this motion, and then try with the other bell in your other hand.

7. Understand that the length of time you spend ringing (and thus, the size of your circle) varies according to the length of the note you are playing. Shorter notes require shorter circles, while longer notes require a wider circle to sustain the sound.

8. Understand your role as a member of a handbell choir. While each person plays a specific set of notes, it's essential to work together as a team to create a cohesive and beautiful sound. Listening to your fellow players and adjusting your technique as necessary is key to a successful performance.

9. Mark your music, if you find it helpful at first. While some players prefer to memorize their parts, others find it helpful to mark their sheet music with indications for when to play each note.

10. Keep the beat. Handbell choirs are often accompanied by a piano or other instrument, and staying in time with the rhythm is essential to creating a polished performance.

11. Have fun. While handbell playing requires discipline and hard work, it's also important to enjoy the process and appreciate the unique beauty of these instruments.

12. Once you have mastered basic handbell playing fundamentals, move on to more advanced techniques. Playing four- or six-in-hand, plucking the bells, and using mallets are all techniques that can add depth and complexity to your playing.

13. Learn to play bells four- and six-in-hand. In these techniques, a single player is responsible for playing multiple bells at once, increasing the range and depth of the music.

14. Try plucking the bells. Plucking produces a softer, more muted sound than ringing, and can be used to create a variety of moods and textures in a piece of music.

15. Try playing with mallets. Mallets can produce a sharp, staccato sound that is distinct from the more sustained sound of ringing or plucking.

16. Venture into the art of solo handbells. While playing solo requires a high level of skill and precision, it can also be a rewarding and beautiful way to showcase your talent and connect with your audience. With practice and dedication, you can become a skilled handbell player and enjoy the unique beauty of these instruments.

Epiphyllum cactus is a unique and beautiful plant that is easy to grow and maintain with proper care. The best way to begin the process of growing an epiphyllum cactus is to obtain a cutting from an existing plant. In this article, we’ll show you how to grow an epiphyllum cactus from a cutting.

Part 1: Obtaining and Storing Epiphyllum Cactus Cuttings

1. Locate an existing epiphyllum cactus plant. Look for a healthy plant with ripe fruit and cut a piece of stem about 6 inches long. Make sure that there are no leaves on the cutting.

2. Store the cutting in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight for 10-14 days. This will allow the cutting to form a thick layer of callus on the cut end.

Part 2: Planting and Cultivating Epiphyllum Cactus Cuttings

3. Plant three cuttings in a 4-inch pot with a drainage hole in the center of the base. Fill the pot with well-draining soil that is slightly acidic.

4. Refrain from watering the cuttings until they have rooted well. This will take about four to six weeks, depending on temperature and humidity conditions.

5. Place the epiphyllum cacti in hanging containers in filtered sunlight. Water your cactus every few days or every day in hot weather.

6. Lightly fertilize your cactus with a time-release fertilizer. This will provide proper nutrition for your plant without overfeeding it.

7. Move your cactus to warmer spots during cold spells. Epiphyllums can tolerate temperatures as low as 40 degrees Fahrenheit, but they grow best in warmer environments.

8. Repot the plants after 1-2 years. This will keep the roots healthy and allow the plant to grow properly.

Part 3: Pruning and Maintenance of Epiphyllum Cactus

9. Disinfect your pruning shears with a bleach-water solution. This will prevent the spread of disease from one plant to another.

10. Clip off flowers after the blossoms expire. This will encourage more growth and keep the plant healthy.

11. Cut all dead, diseased, and broken stems back to the point of origin on the main stem. This will promote healthy growth and prevent the spread of disease.

12. Remove any long stems that disrupt the balance of the epiphyllum. This will keep the plant looking healthy and beautiful.

13. Inspect your cactus for mealybugs, scale insects, and spider mites. These pests can damage the plant and should be addressed immediately.

14. Remove mealybugs and scale insects with cotton swabs dipped in alcohol. Use insecticidal soap to coat the plant. Spray with insecticides to kill bugs and stop serious infestations.

15. Quarantine new plants from infested plants. This will prevent the spread of disease and pests.

By following these tips, you can successfully grow and maintain an epiphyllum cactus and enjoy its unique beauty for many years to come.

How to Replace an Intake Manifold Runner Control Valve on a 96 Ford Windstar

The intake manifold runner control valve on a Ford Windstar helps regulate the airflow in the engine. If the valve fails, it can cause problems with the engine's performance, including reduced power and fuel economy. Fortunately, replacing the valve is a relatively simple process that can be done with just a few tools. Here's how to replace an intake manifold runner control valve on a 96 Ford Windstar.

Step 1: Diagnosis

Before replacing the valve, it's important to diagnose the problem. Check for symptoms such as reduced power, backfiring, and low fuel economy. If the valve is the problem, you may be able to determine this by placing a vacuum gauge on the engine and observing the needle as you rev the engine. If the needle moves erratically, this can be a sign that the valve is not functioning properly.

Step 2: Disconnect the Negative Terminal at the Battery

To prevent any accidental electrical discharge, disconnect your battery by first removing the negative terminal. Make sure your car keys are out of the ignition before proceeding to avoid any sparks.

Step 3: Remove the Accessory Belt

The accessory belt is used to run various components in the engine such as the alternator, power steering and cooling belts. To remove this belt, you need to relieve the tension on the belt by releasing the locking mechanism usually located on the tensioner pulley. Rotate this pulley until the belt loosens.

Step 4: Remove Black Dust Boot from Top of the Alternator

Next, remove the black dust boot from the top of the alternator. This is usually held in place with a simple clip mechanism or Velcro. Wiggle it out gently.

Step 5: Remove the Alternator

Remove the three bolts holding the alternator to the accessory bracket and disconnect the electrical connector on the side of the alternator. This will help you gain access to the valves.

Step 6: Take the Vacuum Lines off of the Fuel Pressure Regulator and Both IMRC Valves

Locate the IMRC valves and remove the vacuum lines that are connected to them, as well as the fuel pressure regulator. These are usually clip-on and can be removed with gentle force and a twisting motion.

Step 7: Remove the White Clip from the Arm of the Valve

The valve is held in place with a white clip which needs to be removed. Gently lift the clip using a screwdriver or pliers and slide it off the arm of the valve.

Step 8: Remove the valve

Remove the valve by wiggling it gently until it comes off the engine block. Take note of the orientation of the valve for re-installation later on.

Step 9: Install the New Valve

Install the new valve, ensuring that it is properly aligned and oriented according to its previous position. Attach the white clip to the valve.

Step 10: Re-install the Accessories

Once you have the new valve installed, re-install all the accessories and wiring you removed earlier, including the alternator, vacuum lines and white clip. Use extreme caution when reinstalling the power steering fluid lines as they are delicate and can break easily.

Step 11: Do a Second Check

Do a final check to ensure that everything is back together properly and none of your tools were left inside the engine compartment before reconnecting the negative terminal to the battery. Test the car to ensure that the engine is running smoothly and all components are working properly.

By following these steps, you can easily replace an intake manifold runner control valve on a 96 Ford Windstar. Regular maintenance and upkeep of your vehicle can help keep it running smoothly and help prevent problems like this from occurring.

Math tests are often a source of stress and anxiety for many students. But, with the right preparation, anyone can perform well on math tests. This article will provide you with tips on how to pass a math test by preparing for class, mastering the material, and practicing good test-taking strategies.

1. Prepare for class.

The first step to doing well on a math test is to be prepared for class. Make sure you attend all your math classes and get the most out of them. Take note of what your teacher emphasizes and the types of problems they assign. If you have questions, don't be afraid to ask. 

2. When you go home, take your notes and/or textbook.

Review the material covered in class as soon as you get home. This will make it easier to remember the new concepts and processes. Read through your notes or textbook, and make sure you understand everything covered in class.

3. Review the new concepts and processes, plus math tables, if any, that you need.

If there are any new concepts or processes that you don't understand, ask your teacher for help. Make sure you also review any math tables that you need to know for the test.

4. Study the math theory.

To do well on a math test, you need to understand the theory behind the problems. Spend some time reviewing the theory and understanding the concepts involved.

5. Eat a good breakfast.

On the day of the test, make sure you eat a good breakfast. Studies have shown that people who eat breakfast perform better on tests than those who don't.

6. Take the test.

When it's time to take the test, read through the instructions carefully and pace yourself accordingly. Don't rush through the problems, but don't spend too much time on any one problem either.

7. Know how to use the whole time allotted for the math test.

Make sure you don't finish the test too quickly. Use all the time given to you to double-check your answers and make sure you didn't make any careless mistakes.

8. Master the art of multiple choice.

If the test includes multiple choice questions, learn how to approach them systematically, eliminating clearly wrong answers and making educated guesses when needed.

9. Master the art of math homework.

Practice, practice, practice. Do as many practice problems as you can, and seek help when you're not sure how to proceed. 

10. After you get the marked test back, review your mistakes.

Once you get your graded test back, review the questions that you got wrong and try to understand why you made the mistake. 

11. Take your math scores to the next level.

To further improve your scores, continue doing your homework until you have mastered all the concepts. Moreover, a week or maximum two weeks before the exam, do extra work each night by redoing every single past homework problem that will be tested on the exam.

12. Experiment, if you have a problem you can't figure out.

If you're struggling with a particular problem, try simplifying it to its easiest form using simple numbers to determine the solution. 

13. Choose between reading the text and getting problems done.

When given the choice, do the problems rather than reading the text. You'll learn more from doing the problems and making mistakes.

14. Learn more than one way to understand the subject.

To truly understand the subject, try to develop depth by learning more than one way to approach it. This will broaden your knowledge and help you tackle any question on the test.

15. Think positively to improve your confidence and effectiveness on the test.

Lastly, maintain a positive attitude towards the test. Believe in yourself and your abilities, and don't let anxiety or fear get in your way. With the right mindset, anyone can pass a math test.

How to Delete Mirar Toolbar

The Mirar Toolbar is a most unwanted add-on to your web browser which seems to invade your system without permission. If you're looking to get rid of it, this article is for you! Follow the steps below to delete Mirar Toolbar once and for all.

Method 1: Using the Registry Editor

1. Click the "Start" button and select "Run," then type "regedit" into the text box if you are using Windows XP.

2. Choose to allow access to the Registry Editor if the screen flashes and a message pops up asking your permission to make changes.

3. Search the folders on the left sidebar and find the folder "Toolbar" under "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE," then "SOFTWARE," then "Microsoft," and finally, "Internet Explorer."

4. Open the folder called "WebBrowser" under the "Toolbar" folder.

5. Find and delete two keys in the "CLSID" folder under "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE," then "SOFTWARE," and then "Classes."

Method 2: Accessing System32 folder

1. Look under the "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE" folder for "SOFTWARE," then "Microsoft," then "Windows," then "CurrentVersion," then "Explorer," and finally, "Browser Help Objects."

2. Reboot your computer by clicking the "Start" button and choosing "Shut down" and then "Restart" if you are using Windows XP.

3. Wait as your computer reboots.

4. Access the System32 folder by typing "cd c:\windows\system32" and hitting the "Enter" key.

5. Open the Control Panel by clicking the "Start" button and choosing "Control Panel."

Congratulations! You have successfully deleted Mirar Toolbar from your system. Enjoy safe browsing!

How to Present an Oral Argument

Presenting an oral argument in a courtroom can be a daunting task, but with the right preparation, you can make a strong case. Whether you’re an experienced attorney or representing yourself, it’s important to understand the purpose of oral argument, review the rules, and thoroughly read all relevant materials. Once you’ve outlined your argument and practiced your delivery, you’ll be ready to stand before the court and make your case. Here’s how:

1. Understand the purpose of oral argument.

Before you begin preparing your argument, it’s important to understand why oral argument is necessary. In general, the purpose of oral argument is to help judges understand the key issues and arguments in a case, and to ask any questions they may have. It’s an opportunity to highlight the strengths of your position and address any weaknesses.

2. Find the court’s list of rules.

Every court has specific rules and guidelines for oral argument, so make sure you review them carefully before you prepare your argument. These rules may cover everything from dress code to time limits and procedures for submitting exhibits. By understanding the rules in advance, you’ll avoid any surprises in the courtroom.

3. Re-read the briefs and the record.

Before you begin outlining your argument, review the briefing and the court record to refresh your memory on the relevant facts and legal issues. This will help you identify any gaps in your knowledge and ensure that you’re fully prepared to address the court’s questions.

4. Re-read all legal authority cited by the parties.

In addition to reviewing the facts, it’s important to review all legal authority cited by the parties, including cases, statutes, and regulations. This will help you address any potential weaknesses in your argument and anticipate any counterarguments.

5. Outline your argument.

Once you’ve reviewed all the materials, outline your argument. This should include a brief summary of the facts, the legal issues at stake, and your key arguments in support of your position. Be sure to organize your arguments in a clear, logical fashion.

6. Create a “cheat sheet” of important facts and legal authority.

To help you stay organized during your argument, create a “cheat sheet” that includes key facts and legal authority. This will enable you to quickly reference important information without having to flip through your materials.

7. Draft a list of questions and answers.

As you outline your argument, anticipate the questions that the judges may ask. Draft a list of potential questions and prepare concise, clear answers.

8. Practice.

Practice delivering your argument out loud, ideally in front of a trusted colleague or mentor who can give you feedback. Rehearsing your argument will help you feel more confident and polished on the day of your oral argument.

9. Listen to sample arguments.

To prepare even further, listen to sample oral arguments online or in person. This will help you understand the pacing and tone of a successful argument and give you more ideas on how to format your presentation.

10. Dress appropriately.

On the day of your argument, dress in a way that is professional and respectful of the court. This will show the judges that you take your case seriously and are prepared to make a strong argument.

11. Turn off your cell phone.

In order to avoid any distractions during your argument, turn off your cell phone or any other devices that might produce noise.

12. Find where you are supposed to sit.

Before the court session begins, locate the position where you will be presenting your argument. This will help you feel more comfortable and prepared when it’s your turn to speak.

13. Speak confidently into the microphone.

Most courtrooms have a microphone to amplify your voice. Speak clearly and confidently into the microphone so that judges can hear your arguments.

14. Introduce yourself to the court.

When you begin your argument, introduce yourself and state your role in the case. Be polite and respectful to the court.

15. Reserve time, if you are the appellant.

If you are the party appealing the case, it’s important to reserve some time for rebuttal at the end of oral arguments. This will allow you to address any new issues that may have arisen during the other party’s presentation.

16. State your requested relief and the grounds.

After you introduce yourself, state your requested relief and the grounds for your request. This should be a concise summary of your argument.

17. Avoid a lengthy recitation of facts.

While it’s important to have a strong grasp of the facts, avoid reciting them at length during your argument. Focus on the key legal issues, rather than getting bogged down in details.

18. Look at the judges.

Maintain eye contact with the judges while you’re speaking. This will help you build a connection with them and show that you’re confident in your arguments.

19. Stand still.

While it can be tempting to pace or fidget, try to stand still while you’re presenting. This will help you appear confident and composed.

20. Try to avoid using exhibits.

In most cases, it’s best to rely on your oral argument rather than long exhibits. This will help you keep the pace of your argument moving and avoid losing the judges’ attention.

21. Raise all of your arguments.

During your argument, make sure to raise all of your key arguments. This will help you ensure that you’ve covered all relevant issues and strengthen your overall position.

22. Understand the question before answering.

If a judge asks you a question, take a moment to understand the specific issue they’re raising before answering. This will help you avoid confusion or misunderstandings.

23. Answer the question asked.

When you’re answering a judge’s question, focus on the specific issue they’ve raised rather than trying to steer the conversation back to your main argument.

24. Correct inaccuracies and mis-impressions.

If a judge has a misunderstanding of the facts or legal issues, be sure to correct it clearly and politely.

25. Don’t talk over the judge.

While it’s important to make your case, it’s also important to respect the judges’ authority. Don’t talk over them or interrupt them while they’re speaking.

26. Offer supplemental briefing.

If there’s an issue that you weren’t able to fully address during oral argument, offer to provide supplemental briefing to the court.

27. Listen closely.

As other parties present their arguments, listen closely to what they’re saying. This will help you identify potential weaknesses in your own argument or anticipate questions from the judges.

28. List the appellee’s strongest arguments.

During your rebuttal period, list the appellee’s strongest arguments and provide a concise rebuttal.

29. Jot down counterarguments.

During oral argument, take notes on any counterarguments that may arise so you’re prepared to address them.

30. Rank the arguments in importance.

Prioritize the arguments you’ve outlined based on their strength and importance.

31. Summarize the argument, then rebut.

At the end of oral argument, summarize the key points of your argument and then provide a concise rebuttal to the other party’s position.

By following these steps, you’ll be well on your way to presenting a strong and effective oral argument in court. Remember to stay calm, focused, and respectful, and you’ll increase your chances of success.

Driving a manual car can be a fun and rewarding experience, but it can also be daunting for beginners. Learning to drive a manual car requires some patience and a lot of practice. However, with the right guidance and a little bit of hard work, anyone can learn how to drive a manual car.

Starting on level ground with the car off.

Before you even start the car, make sure that you are on a completely level surface with the car off. This will help you get accustomed to the feel of the clutch and the gear stick without worrying about the car moving.

Learn what the clutch does.

The clutch is a pedal located to the left of the brake pedal. Its main function is to disconnect the engine from the transmission, allowing you to switch gears. It's important to understand how the clutch works before you start driving. Practice pressing the clutch pedal in and out while the car is off to get used to the feel of it.

Adjust the seat position so you can access the clutch pedal’s full range of motion.

Make sure that you adjust your seat position so that you can comfortably reach the clutch pedal without having to really stretch your leg. You should also make sure that you can fully depress the clutch pedal without having to contort your leg or foot.

Press the clutch pedal and hold it to the floor.

Start by pressing the clutch pedal all the way down to the floor with your left foot. This will disconnect the engine from the transmission and allow you to switch gears. Make sure you hold the clutch down to the floor while you move the gear stick.

Move the gear stick into neutral.

With the clutch still all the way down, move the gear stick into the middle position- which is neutral. This is indicated on most manual cars by a small line on the gauge, or by a letter (N).

Start the engine with the key in the ignition, making sure the gear stick is still in neutral.

Once the gear stick is in neutral, turn the key in the ignition to start the engine. Make sure that the gear stick is still in neutral otherwise your car might move when starting the engine.

Remove your foot from the clutch pedal with the car still in neutral.

After the engine has started, remove your foot from the clutch pedal with the car still in neutral. This should be done gently and not too fast.

Press the clutch to the floor and move the gearstick into first gear.

With the car still running, press the clutch pedal all the way to the floor and move the gearstick into first gear. This gear should have a notch or an H shape on the gauge.

Slowly lift your foot up from the clutch pedal.

As you slowly lift your foot up from the clutch pedal, the car will start to move forward. You should focus on controlling the speed with the clutch and not the accelerator.

Let up on the clutch while pushing down on the accelerator.

As you move forward, you should start to let up on the clutch while pushing down on the accelerator pedal with your right foot. This will help you control the speed of the car.

Expect to stall at least a few times when you’re first starting out.

Stalling is a normal part of the learning process when it comes to driving a manual car. Don't get discouraged if you stall a few times in the beginning.

Recognize when it’s time to shift up to a higher gear.

As you gain speed, you'll need to shift up to a higher gear. A good rule of thumb is to shift up when your engine reaches about 2,500 to 3,000 RPMs.

Push down on the accelerator very slightly and slowly release the clutch pedal.

When shifting gears, you should push down on the accelerator very slightly while slowly releasing the clutch pedal. This will help you maintain a smooth transition between gears.

Shift down into a lower gear as you slow down.

As you slow down, you'll need to shift down into a lower gear. A good rule of thumb is to shift down when your engine reaches about 1,500 RPMs.

Come to a complete stop.

When you're ready to stop, push the clutch pedal all the way down and move the gear stick into neutral. Then, bring the car to a complete stop.

Practice on an easy course with an experienced manual driver.

It can be helpful to practice on an easy course with an experienced manual driver. This will help you gain confidence and get used to driving a manual car.

Avoid stopping and starting on steep hills initially.

Starting and stopping on steep hills can be challenging for even experienced manual drivers. It's a good idea to avoid these situations until you get more comfortable.

Learn parking procedures, especially on hills.

Parking a manual car on a hill requires some skill and practice. Make sure you learn the correct parking procedures before attempting to park on a hill.

Stop completely before changing from forward to reverse (and vice versa).

To switch from forward to reverse or vice versa, you should always come to a complete stop before doing so. This will help avoid any potential accidents or damage to the transmission.

Driving a manual car can be a fun and rewarding experience, but it takes time and practice to master. By following these tips and practicing regularly, you'll be well on your way to becoming a skilled manual driver.

If you want to give your kitchen a sleek, modern look without breaking the bank, you can fake stainless steel appliances with contact paper. This project is easy, fun, and can be done on a budget. Here's how you can fake stainless steel appliances in just a few simple steps.

1. Buy Some Stainless Steel Contact Paper

How to Sharpen a Kitchen Knife

If you're tired of using a dull kitchen knife, it's time to sharpen it! Sharpening a kitchen knife isn't difficult, but it does require some patience and focus. In this article, we'll break down the process into manageable steps to ensure your knife is razor-sharp and ready to go.

Gather the necessary materials.

Before you start, you'll need a few materials:

- A whetstone (also known as a sharpening stone)
- Water
- A bowl or container to soak the whetstone in
- A non-slip surface (such as a damp towel or a rubber mat) to place the whetstone on
- A wooden cutting board to test the sharpness of the knife
- A honing rod (optional)

Soak your whetstones in water until no air bubbles pop up anymore.

Most whetstones need to be soaked in water before use. Submerge your whetstone in water until no more bubbles come up to the surface. The amount of time it takes will vary depending on the type of whetstone you have, but 10-20 minutes is generally a good rule of thumb.

Place the stone on a non-slip service to prevent any dangerous issues.

When you're ready to begin, place your whetstone on a non-slip surface. This will prevent the stone from moving around while you're sharpening your knife.

Begin with the course grit side of the stone, the one with the lower number.

Whetstones usually have two sides: a coarser grit for sharpening and a finer grit for honing. Start with the coarse grit side of the stone, which is typically numbered lower.

Tilt the knife so that the blade makes a roughly 22-degree angle with the stone.

The angle of the knife is important when sharpening. A rough rule to follow is to tilt the blade so that it forms a roughly 22-degree angle with the stone. You can do this by holding the knife at a slight angle to the stone and adjusting until it feels right.

Hold the knife with the handle in your dominant hand so that your index finger is on the edge of the blade, almost where it meets the stone.

With the knife in your dominant hand, grip the handle firmly and place your index finger on the backside of the blade.

Spread your non-dominant hand fingers on the back of the blade itself, applying even pressure across the whole blade down into the stone.

With your non-dominant hand, place your fingers on the back of the blade, applying even pressure as you sharpen.

Keeping the angle of the knife consistent throughout, push the blade evenly across the whetstone.

Maintain the angle of the knife and move it across the whetstone in a smooth, even motion. Make sure to apply equal pressure across the blade.

Splash the whetstone with water every few minutes to keep it wet.

As you work, splash a little water onto the surface of the whetstone to keep it wet. This will help to prevent the blade from overheating and keep the sharpening process smooth and consistent.

Repeat as many times as necessary, moving your fingers across the blade to sharpen the whole thing.

Continue sharpening until you're happy with the blade's sharpness. You may need to repeat the process several times, depending on how dull the knife is.

Flip the blade over and repeat with the other side, making the same number of passes.

Once you've sharpened one side of the blade, flip the knife over and repeat the process on the other side. Make sure to keep the same number of passes on each side.

Switch to the finer grit stone and alternate sharpening each side.

When you're satisfied with the sharpness of your knife, switch to the finer grit side of the whetstone and repeat the process, alternating between each side of the blade.

"Cut" a wooden cutting board with the knife to even out the cutting surface.

To ensure the blade is sharp all the way across, cut into a wooden cutting board a few times.

Hone the blade.

If you have a honing rod, use it to hone the blade. Run the blade along the rod in the same angle you used to sharpen it, using light pressure.

And there you have it - your kitchen knife is sharpened and ready to go! With a little practice, you'll be able to keep your knives sharp all the time.

Quillows are versatile and practical items that combine the comfort of a quilt with the convenience of a pillow. They are perfect for use as blankets on chilly nights or as pillows during travel. Making your own quillow may seem daunting, but it is actually a straightforward process that can be accomplished with some fabric, batting, and thread. Follow these steps to learn how to make a quillow.

Part 1 of 3: Select Your Materials

1. Select your fabric. Choose a sturdy and lightweight fabric for your quillow. Cotton is an excellent option for its durability and comfort. You'll need enough fabric to create a blanket that's at least 4 feet by 4 feet. If you desire a larger quillow, purchase additional fabric accordingly.

2. Select your batting. Batting is the layer that goes between the two pieces of fabric in your quillow. It adds warmth and thickness to the blanket. There are different types of batting to choose from, but a lightweight polyester batting works well.

3. Buy thread that matches your pattern. Choose a thread that matches the colors in your fabric pattern. It's important to have thread that blends in and doesn't stand out.

4. Trim your fabric to the desired size. Lay out your fabric on a flat surface and measure it to your desired size. Use a rotary cutter, fabric scissors, and a ruler to trim your fabric to the correct dimensions.

Part 2 of 3: Construct Your Quilt

1. Lay the fabric down, one piece on top of the other, with the right sides touching each other. This forms the outside of the quillow.

2. Lay the batting on top of the two pieces of fabric, then pin the edges of the three layers together. Trim the batting to the exact size of the fabric, if it is not already the same size.

3. Stitch the three layers together with a 1⁄2 inch (1.3 cm) seam, taking care to not sew the 12 inch (30.5 cm) opening closed. Remove the pins.

4. Turn the blanket right-side out through the 12 inch (30.5 cm) opening.

5. Sew a 1/4 inch seam around all four edges of the quilt, closing the 12 inch (30.5 cm) opening.

Part 3 of 3: Make Your Pillow Pocket

1. Fold the 1⁄2 yard (0.5 m) fabric in half, right sides facing each other, and stitch the long edges of the rectangle together with a 1⁄2 inch (1.3 cm) seam.

2. Turn the blanket right-side out through the open side of the pillow pocket.

3. Sew a 1/4 inch seam to close the open edge only; do not stitch the way around the pocket.

4. Lay the larger, main blanket on a flat surface and lay the pillow pocket at the top center of the blanket.

5. Sew the three outer edges of the pillow pocket to the blanket using a 1⁄4 inch (0.6 cm) seam.

6. Lay the blanket on the ground, pocket side down.

7. Fold the outer edges of the blanket to the opposite edges of the pocket.

8. Fold the blanket up from the bottom, once again into thirds. The blanket should now be folded to the dimensions of the pillow pocket.

9. Flip pocket over the blanket. Smooth the edges and fluff for a perfect pillow.

10. Convert back to a blanket by simply flipping and unfolding the blanket.

Congratulations! You have now successfully made a quillow. Customize your quillow with your choice of fabric and batting to create a warm and cozy addition to your home or travel essentials.

Sky lanterns are a popular way to create an enchanting ambiance during celebrations or events. While it may seem daunting to make one from scratch at home, it can actually be a fun and easy DIY project. Here is how you can make your own sky lanterns.

Materials:
- Lightweight, non-flammable fabric cut into a square of approximately 36" x 36" (90cm x 90cm)
- Florist's wire, cut into two 24" (60cm) pieces
- Candle wax
- Aluminum foil, cut into a strip of 3" x 1" (7.5cm x 2.5cm)
- Bamboo skewers, cut into halves
- Non-flammable tape
- Kitchen paper towel or tissue paper cut into 4" x 4" (10cm x 10cm) pieces
- Fireproofing spray
- Brown craft paper
- Non-flammable glue
- Paper bag

Instructions:

1. Start by tying the fabric into a tight knot.

2. Center the two 24" (60cm) pieces of florist's wire over the knot.

3. Wrap the wire around the knot, and twist them tightly to make them secure.

4. Place the candle over a lighter or other open flame until the wax melts down into a liquid state.

5. Place the knot into the hot, melted wax and let it soak for three to five minutes.

6. Remove the newly created wick from the wax.

7. Wrap the aluminum-foil strip around the knot in the center of the wick.

8. Cut three bamboo skewers in half lengthwise using either a razor blade or a utility knife.

9. Line the split bamboo up end to end on a table to make a single long strip.

10. Secure the overlapping connection points together with non-flammable tape.

11. Tape the ends of the foil-wrapped wires that protrude from the wick to opposite sides of the bamboo frame.

12. Hang 16-20 pieces of kitchen paper towel (or about half that of tissue paper) on a clothesline using clothespins (pegs). Place a plastic or canvas drop cloth under the paper to catch any drippings.

13. Spray both sides of each piece of paper thoroughly with the fireproofing spray.

14. Draw a vertical line 40" (about 1 meter) long down the center of the brown craft paper.

15. Draw a horizontal line 12" (30cm) long at the base of the vertical line.

16. Draw a second horizontal line that is 22" (1/2 meter) long approximately two thirds of the way up the vertical line.

17. Connect the two horizontal lines by sketching a line that curves gently inward before meeting the vertical line.

18. Draw a second line mirroring the line that you just drew to connect the left tips of the two horizontal lines.

19. Sketch mirroring lines that connect each end of the upper horizontal line to the top of the vertical line.

20. Cut the shape that you've drawn out of the brown craft paper using scissors.

21. Lay the 16-20 fireproofed paper pieces on a flat surface.

22. Use a non-flammable glue to seal the overlapped ends of the papers together.

23. Lay one 2-piece panel of paper towel/tissue paper over the brown craft paper pattern.

24. Repeat this step with the remaining 2-piece paper panels.

25. Connect the pointed tips of the paper towel/tissue paper panels together.

26. Attach the opening of the paper bag to the bamboo frame.

27. Fold the end of the paper bag upward to cover the frame.

28. Take your lantern outside at night or at dusk.

Enjoy the unique and mesmerizing glow of your handmade sky lanterns as they drift up into the sky. Remember to take proper safety precautions and check local regulations before launching your sky lanterns.

Creating a collage of Polaroids using Photoshop CS5 is a fun and creative way to display your favorite memories. With this guide, you can easily learn how to create a beautiful collage of Polaroids using Photoshop CS5.

Step 1: Choose your Photos

The first step in creating a Polaroid collage is to choose the photos you want to include in your collage. Once you have selected the photos, open them in Photoshop CS5.

Step 2: Duplicate the Background Layers

After you have chosen which picture you are going to collage and have opened it within Photoshop CS5, you'll need to duplicate the background layers. To do this, simply right-click on the background layer and select "Duplicate Layer."

Step 3: Add a Blank Layer

Add a blank layer between the background layer and layer 1. To do this, click on "Layer" in the top menu and select "New" and then select "Layer."

Step 4: Fill the New Layer with Black

Fill the new layer as black, the foreground color. To do this, select the Paint Bucket Tool from the left side toolbar and click on the new layer to fill it with black.

Step 5: Create Layer 3

With layer 2 selected, click on the new layer icon again to create Layer 3.

Step 6: Select the Rectangular Marquee Tool

Select the rectangular marquee tool from the sidebar on the left.

Step 7: Fill the Selection with Black

Fill the selection from step 5 with black. To do this, select the Paint Bucket Tool and click inside the rectangular selection to fill it with black.

Step 8: Create a Clipping Mask

Now we need to create a clipping mask using the selection we just filled with black in step 6. To do this, right-click on Layer 3 and select "Create Clipping Mask."

Step 9: Add Another Blank Layer

Now we need to add another new blank layer above layer 2. To do this, click on "Layer" in the top menu and select "New" and then select "Layer."

Step 10: Select the Rectangular Marquee Tool Again

Now select the rectangular marquee tool again from the left side toolbar and drag out the border of the Polaroid photo around the first inside Polaroid image.

Step 11: Fill the Selected Section with White

We want to fill the selected section with white, thus looking like a Polaroid picture. To do this, select the Paint Bucket Tool and click inside the selection to fill it with white.

Step 12: Rotate the Photo

To give the photo a more realistic collage look, we can rotate it however we'd like. To do this, select the Move Tool and hover over the edges of the photo until you see the rotation icon, then click and drag to rotate the photo.

Step 13: Group the Layers

Now we need to group the three layers that makeup the Polaroid picture, layers 1, 3, and 4. To do this, select all three layers by holding down the Shift key, then right-click and select "Group Layers."

Step 14: Duplicate the Layer Group

Now we want to create more Polaroids that are the same shape and size of our original one, so we want to duplicate this layer group. To do this, right-click on the layer group and select "Duplicate Group."

Step 15: Repeat Steps 13 and 14

Expand this folder and select both layers 3 and 4 (holding down shift to select both) and then with these two selected hold down command+T. Repeat steps 13 and 14 until you have gathered a collage of Polaroids.

Congratulations! You have successfully created a beautiful collage of Polaroids using Photoshop CS5.

Introducing yourself in a new language can feel daunting, but with a little practice, it becomes easier over time. If you want to introduce yourself in Irish, start by learning the basics of self-introduction and how to ask someone else who they are. This article will also cover how to say your name, ask for someone's name, and explain your age depending on your age group. Additionally, you'll learn how to say where you're from and ask someone else where they're from. Finally, we'll go over some common professions so you can tell someone what you do.

Part 1: Introducing Yourself and Asking Who Someone Else Is

1. To introduce yourself in Irish, say "Is mise" (Iss mish-ah), followed by your name. For example, "Is mise Aoife" (Iss mish-ah Ee-fah) means "I am Aoife."

2. To ask who someone else is, say "Cé tusa?" (kay too-sa), which means "Who are you?"

Part 2: Saying Your Name and Asking for Someone's Name

1. To say your name, say "Is ainm dom" (Iss annum dum), which means "My name is." For example, "Is ainm dom Conall" (Iss annum dum Kun-all) means "My name is Conall."

2. You can also say "Is é an t-ainm atá orm" (Iss ay on tannum ah-taw urm), which means "My name is." For example, "Is é an t-ainm atá orm Niamh" (Iss ay on tannum ah-taw urm nee-uv) means "My name is Niamh."

3. To ask someone's name, say "Cad is ainm duit?" (kad iss annum dit), which means "What is your name?"

Part 3: Explaining Your Age Depending on Your Age Group

1. To say your age if you're 1 or 2 years old or younger, say "Tá mé aon bhliain d'aois" (Taw may ayn vlee-inn deesh), which means "I am one year old."

2. To say your age if you're 3-6 years old, say "Tá mé trí bliana d'aois" (Taw may tree bleen-ah deesh), which means "I am three years old." Replace "trí" with "ceithre" (cah-her-ah) for four, "cúig" (coo-ig) for five, or "sé" (shay) for 6.

3. To say your age if you're 7-10 years old, say "Tá mé seacht mbliana d'aois"(Taw may shocked bleen-ah deesh), which means "I am seven years old." Replace "seacht" (shocked) with "ocht" for eight, "naoi" (knee) for nine, or "deich" (deh) for 10.

4. To say your age if you're 11-19, use the same basic approach but replace the "ten" part with "deich" (deh). For example, "Tá mé deich n-aon mbliana d'aois" (Taw may deh nayn bleen-ah deesh) means "I am eleven years old."

5. If you're 21-29, replace "d'aois" with "fiche (fih-ha)." For example, "Tá mé fiche a haon mbliana d'aois" (Taw may fih-ha ayn bleen-ah deesh) means "I am twenty-one years old."

6. If you're 31-39, replace "d'aois" with "triocha" (truck-ah). For example, "Tá mé triocha a cúig mbliana d'aois" (Taw may truck-ah a coo-ig bleen-ah deesh) means "I am thirty-five years old."

7. If you're 41-49, replace "d'aois" with "daichead" (doh-had). For example, "Tá mé daichead a sé mbliana d'aois" (Taw may doh-had a shay bleen-ah deesh) means "I am forty-six years old."

8. If you're 51-59, replace "d'aois" with "caoga" (cway-gah). For example, "Tá mé caoga a trí mbliana d'aois" (Taw may cway-gah a tree bleen-ah deesh) means "I am fifty-three years old."

9. If you're 61-69, replace "d'aois" with "seasca" (shask-ah). For example, "Tá mé seasca a hocht mbliana d'aois" (Taw may shask-ah a hocked bleen-ah deesh) means "I am sixty-eight years old."

10. If you're 71-79, replace "d'aois" with "seachtó" (shock-toe). For example, "Tá mé seachtó a naoi mbliana d'aois" (Taw may shock-toe a knee bleen-ah deesh) means "I am seventy-nine years old."

11. If you're 81-89, replace "d'aois" with "ochtó" (ucked-oh). For example, "Tá mé ochtó a trí mbliana d'aois" (Taw may ucked-oh a tree bleen-ah deesh) means "I am eighty-three years old."

12. If you're 91-99, replace "d'aois" with "nócha" (noke-ah). For example, "Tá mé nócha a sé mbliana d'aois" (Taw may noke-ah a shay bleen-ah deesh) means "I am ninety-six years old."

Part 4: Saying Where You're From and Asking Where Someone Else Is From

1. To say where you're from, say "Is as mé" (Iss oss may), followed by your hometown or country. For example, "Is as Baile Átha Cliath mé" (Iss oss Bal-ya aa-aha clee-ah may) means "I am from Dublin."

2. To ask where someone else is from, say "Cárb as thú?" (kawr-ib oss hoo), which means "Where are you from?"

Part 5: Common Professions

1. Farmer - Feirmeoir (Fer-myore)
2. Shopkeeper - Siopadóir (Shup-adore)
3. Policeman (Irish police are referred to as the Guards) - Garda (Gard-ah)
4. Doctor - Dochtúir (Duck-ture)
5. Teacher - Múinteoir (Moo-in-chore)
6. Nurse - Altra (Oltra)
7. Dentist - Fiaclóir (Fee-ah-clore)
8. Psychologist - Síceolaí (She-coal-ee)
9. Pharmacist - Cógaiseoir (Coe-gah-sore)
10. Fisherman - Iascaire (Eess-currah)
11. Vet - Tréidlia (Trade-lia)
12. Author - Scíbhneoir (Shcreev-nore)
13. Singer - Amhránaí (Ow-raw-knee)
14. Actor - Aisteoir (Ash-tore)
15. Architect - Ailtire (All-turr-ah)
16. Builder - Tógálaí (Tow-gawl-ee)
17. Mechanic - Meicneoir (Meck-nore)
18. Chauffeur - Tiománaí (Tim-aw-knee)
19. Child-minder - Feighlí Leanaí (Fye-lee lanny)

Writing a request for proposal (RFP) can be a daunting task, but with the right preparation and organization, you can make it an effective tool for finding the right consultant or contractor for your project. Here are some steps to follow when writing an RFP that will get you the results you want.

1. Know what you want.

Before you start writing your RFP, you need to have a clear idea of what you want to achieve with your project. Ask yourself what your goals and mission are, and what specific outcomes you hope to achieve. This will help you narrow down your search for the right consultant or contractor.

2. Assess your goals and mission.

After you have a good understanding of what you want to achieve, assess your goals and mission in more detail. Consider what kind of expertise and experience you need to achieve your goals, and what kind of approach you want your consultant or contractor to take.

3. Determine your budget.

Before you start looking for potential bidders, you need to know how much money you have to spend on your project. Your budget will help you determine what kind of consultant or contractor you can afford, and what kind of services you can expect.

4. Put together a timeline.

To help you keep track of your project, put together a timeline that outlines key milestones and deadlines. This will help you stay on track throughout the project and make sure you are making progress towards your goals.

5. Read other RFPs.

To get a sense of what kind of information to include in your RFP, read other RFPs that are similar to yours. This will give you an idea of the questions you should ask and the kind of information you should provide.

6. Establish the projected scope and boundaries of your project.

Make sure you know what you are looking for in terms of the scope and boundaries of your project. This will help potential bidders understand what they are getting into and make sure you are on the same page.

7. List your "must haves" and your "like to haves."

Make a list of your needs and wants, and differentiate between your "must haves" and your "like to haves." This will make it easier for potential bidders to understand your needs and provide you with relevant proposals.

8. Decide who will read the proposals and award the project.

Determine which individuals will read and evaluate the proposals that come in, and who will ultimately make the decision about which bidder to select.

9. Specify a candidate's minimum qualifications.

Provide a list of minimum qualifications that potential bidders must meet. This will help you ensure that you are working with qualified and competent consultants or contractors.

10. Draft a scorecard that you will use to evaluate proposals.

Create a scorecard that you will use to evaluate proposals based on your goals, objectives, and other criteria.

11. Include all relevant details.

Provide all of the relevant details about your project, including timelines, budgets, objectives, and other pertinent information.

12. Be specific, but not too specific.

Be specific about your needs and requirements, but avoid being too prescriptive. Leave room for bidders to propose solutions that are tailored to your needs.

13. Organize the RFP effectively.

Organize your RFP in a clear and concise manner, using subheadings and bullet points to make the information easy to navigate.

14. Request references.

Ask potential bidders to provide references from past clients, so you can assess their track record and level of expertise.

15. Proofread your RFP before sending it out.

Make sure to proofread your RFP before sending it out, to ensure it is clear, concise, and free of errors.

16. Send RFPs to reputable consulting firms.

Send your RFPs to reputable consulting firms that have experience and expertise in your area of need.

17. Limit the number of firms or individuals you send your RFP to.

Limit the number of firms or individuals you send your RFP to, to ensure you are able to manage the responses you receive.

18. Give an adequate amount of time for individuals to put together a quality proposal.

Give potential bidders enough time to put together a thorough and detailed proposal that reflects your needs and requirements.

19. Stick to your deadline.

Make sure to stick to your deadline for receiving and evaluating proposals, so you can move forward with your project in a timely and efficient manner.

Neutral operations with square roots may seem complex, but with the help of Excel and a few formula steps, you can easily handle these equations. Here's a step by step guide to performing neutral operations with square roots using Excel:

Part 1: Setting up the Worksheet
1. Open a new workbook in Excel from the desktop, dock or within your Applications folder inside the Microsoft folder.
2. In Preferences, set R1C1 to unchecked or Off, set Ribbon to checked or On, set Show Formula Bar to checked or On and set Calculation to .000 000 000 000 001 (without interim spaces) and 100 iterations and Calculate Automatically.
3. Click on the far upper left top corner above the 1 of row 1 and to the left of column A.
4. Title the first worksheet, "NeuOps sqrt(n)" and save the workbook as "Do Neu Ops w Sqrts" into an appropriate folder such as 'Microsoft Excel Imagery', 'Neu Ops' or 'wikiHow Articles'
5. Enter the Row 1 and Row 2 Headings as follows:

- Enter to cell A1, a
- Enter to cell A2, By changing cell
- Enter to cell B1, sqrt(a)
- Enter to cell C1, sqrt(b)
- Enter to cell C2, " = sqrt(a)/(sqrt(a)-1)" (without quotes and with a leading space)
- Enter to cell D1, b =
- Enter to cell D2, (sqrt(b))^2
- Enter to cell E1, c =
- Enter to cell E2, sqrt(a) + sqrt(b)
- Enter to cell F1, c =
- Enter to cell F2, sqrt(a) * sqrt(b)
- Enter to cell G1, Goal
- Enter to cell H1, Goal Seek to 0

6. Enter the algebraic solution to the problem sqrt(a)+sqrt(b)=sqrt(a)*sqrt(b) in column I.
7. Format the Goal Seeking columns in red.
8. Define variable names for the worksheet. Select columns A to C and do Insert Name Create in Top Row. You should end up with 3 variable names: a, sqrt_a and sqrt_b.
9. Enter the Input cells and formulas for rows 3-5 as follows:

- Enter to cell A3 the formula, =PI()
- Enter to cell A4 the formula, =10
- Enter to cell A5 the value, 1, as a preliminary guess.

10. Do Goal Seeking to 2π. Enter to cell G5 the formula, =2*PI() and Format Cells Fill yellow. Enter to cell H5 the formula, =G5-F5. Select cell H5 and do Tools, Goal Seek, Set Cell H5, To value 0, By changing cell, and click on cell A5. Select cell range A1:I5 and Edit Copy it and Edit Paste it to A8:I12.
11. Modify the algebraic solution. Enter to cell I8, sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)=sqrt(a)*sqrt(b), and follow the steps:

- Enter to cell I9, sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)+sqrt(b)=(sqrt(a)*sqrt(b))+sqrt(b).
- Enter to cell I10, sqrt(a)=sqrt(b)*(sqrt(a)+1).
- Enter to cell I11, sqrt(a)/(sqrt(a)+1)=sqrt(b).

12. Edit in the formula bar cell I11 and copy just the part that reads sqrt(a)/(sqrt(a)+1) and Edit Paste it to cell C9. Change the formulas appropriately by entering to cell C10 the formula, =sqrt_a/(sqrt_a+1), and Edit Fill Down to cell C12. Do Goal Seeking to 2π by selecting cell H12 and doing Tools, Goal Seek, Set Cell H12, To value 0, By changing cell, and click on cell A12.

Part 2: Modifying the Algebraic Solution
1. Select cell range A1:I12 and Edit Copy it and Edit Paste it to A14:I25.
2. Modify the algebraic solution by entering to cell I14, sqrt(a)+sqrt(b)=sqrt(a)/sqrt(b), and follow the steps:

- Enter to cell I15, sqrt(a)+sqrt(b)-sqrt(a)=(sqrt(a)/sqrt(b))-sqrt(a).
- Enter to cell I16, sqrt(b)=sqrt(a)/(1/(sqrt(b)) - 1).
- Enter to cell I17, sqrt(b)/(1/(sqrt(b)) - 1)=sqrt(a).

3. Edit in the formula bar cell I17 and copy just the part that reads sqrt(b)/(1/(sqrt(b)) - 1) and Edit Paste it to cell B15. 
4. Change the formulas appropriately by entering to cell B16 the formula, =sqrt_b/(1/(sqrt_b)-1), and Edit Fill Down to cell B18. 
5. Do Goal Seeking to -2π by entering to cell G18 the formula, =-2*PI(), and selecting cell H18. Do Tools, Goal Seek, Set Cell H18, To value 0, By changing cell, and click on cell A18.

Following these steps will help you perform neutral operations with square roots using Excel. With practice, you'll be able to handle these complex equations with ease and efficiency.

How to Create a Photography Portfolio

If you're a photographer looking to showcase your work and attract potential clients, one of the best ways to do so is by creating a photography portfolio. But how do you go about creating a portfolio that truly showcases your skills and stands out from the crowd? In this article, we'll guide you through the steps necessary to create an impressive photography portfolio that accurately represents your style and skills.

1. Identify the Purpose of Your Portfolio

Before you begin creating your portfolio, it's important to consider the purpose behind it. Whether you're creating a portfolio to attract potential clients or to show your work in a gallery, specifying the purpose of your portfolio will give you a solid idea about who your audience is and how you should present your work.

2. Consider Your Audience

Once you've identified the purpose of your portfolio, it's important to consider your audience. Who will be viewing your portfolio? What type of photography are they interested in? Answering these questions will help you decide on the best format and content for your portfolio.

3. Decide on a Unifying Theme

In most cases, your portfolio doesn’t need to showcase the best of your entire body of work. Instead, it should focus on a specific theme or concept that ties your images together. Choose a theme that accurately represents your style and skills.

4. Choose a Portfolio Format

There are many different formats you can choose for your portfolio, from traditional paper-based portfolios to modern digital portfolios. Consider the preferences of your audience and the purpose of your portfolio when choosing a format.

5. Go Through Your Body of Work

Once you've narrowed down your focus and chosen a format, it's time to go through your body of work and choose the images that best represent your chosen concept.

6. Assess the Quality of Each Photo Individually

As you examine each image, think about whether or not it represents your chosen concept. Does it accurately showcase your skills and style? Is it of high quality?

7. Be Consistent

When choosing your images, make sure they're consistent in terms of quality, style, and theme.

8. Remove Any Flawed or Repetitive Images

Get rid of images that are out of focus, that have visible flaws, or that are too similar to other images in your portfolio.

9. Get the Opinion of Someone You Trust

It's important to be able to evaluate your own work critically, but it will be difficult to be completely objective. Get the opinion of someone you trust to help you choose the best images for your portfolio.

10. Settle on Ten to Twenty Final Images

There isn't a specific number of images a portfolio should include and opinions about this tend to vary. Choose the number of images that accurately represent your skills and style without overwhelming your audience.

11. Tweak Your Final Images if Necessary

Before putting your final images into your portfolio, make any necessary tweaks in post-processing to ensure they're of the highest quality.

12. Organize the Images into a Particular Sequence

There is no “right” way to order your images, but you should consider the impact of the presentation on your audience. Think about the flow of images and how they work together to tell a story.

13. Use High Quality Materials

Invest in high quality materials that will showcase your work in the best light. Consider using high-quality paper, ink, and printing services.

14. Put the Photos into Your Portfolio

Once your images are complete and your portfolio format is chosen, it's time to put everything together.

15. Add the Finishing Touches

The amount of additional information you include in your portfolio is up to you. Consider adding an artist statement or a brief bio to help your audience understand your work and your style.

16. Consider an Online Portfolio

In addition to a traditional portfolio, consider creating an online portfolio that you can share with potential clients and your network. This can be a great way to expand your reach and showcase your work to a larger audience.

By following these steps, you'll be well on your way to creating an impressive photography portfolio that showcases your skills and attracts potential clients.
